## Getting Started

Set up your notebook with the usual ritual:

1. **Create a new notebook** (`+` → **Notebook** → **eds217_2026**).
2. **Rename it** to `Session_1D_Whole_Game_2.ipynb`.
3. **Add a title cell** (Markdown), updating the date:

```markdown
# Day 1: Session 1D - The Whole Game, Part 2

[Session Webpage](https://eds-217-essential-python.github.io/course-materials/interactive-sessions/1d_whole_game_2.html)

Date: 08/31/2026
```

### Pick up where Part 1 left off

We are in a fresh notebook, so first re-run the workflow from Part 1 to rebuild `df` and
`monthly_means`.

✅ **Canonical cell. Copy and run it exactly:**

```{python}
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/EDS-217-Essential-Python/EDS-217-Essential-Python.github.io/refs/heads/main/data/toolik_weather.csv"
df = pd.read_csv(url)

monthly = df.groupby('Month')
monthly_means = monthly['Daily_AirTemp_Mean_C'].mean()
```

## Step 6: Visualize 📊

**Visualize** means turning numbers into a picture you can read quickly. The simplest
plot is a line plot with `plt.plot()`.

✅ **Canonical cell. Copy and run it exactly:**

```{python}
plt.plot(monthly_means)
plt.title("Toolik Monthly Temperatures")
plt.xlabel("Month")
plt.ylabel("Temperature (°C)")
plt.show()
```

The same twelve numbers now show a clear seasonal cycle. We can also draw them as bars
with `plt.bar()`. Copy the first line exactly. The month numbers for the x-axis come straight
from your `monthly_means`.

```{python}
plt.bar(monthly_means.index, monthly_means)
plt.title("Toolik Monthly Temperatures")
plt.xlabel("Month")
plt.ylabel("Temperature (°C)")
plt.show()
```

:::{.callout-tip title="🔁 Change one thing"}
Change only a label. The data stays exactly the same. Pick one new title from this menu and
re-run:

- `plt.title("Average Temperature by Month")`
- `plt.title("Arctic Seasonality at Toolik")`
- `plt.title("Monthly Mean Air Temperature, 1988 to 2018")`

You could reword the `plt.ylabel(...)` text instead. Either way, change just one thing.
:::

```{python}
# 🔁 Example: same plot, one new label. The data (monthly_means) stays the same.
plt.bar(monthly_means.index, monthly_means)
plt.title("Arctic Seasonality at Toolik")
plt.xlabel("Month")
plt.ylabel("Temperature (°C)")
plt.show()
```

:::{.callout-important title="✍️ Say it in a sentence (required)"}
Read the coldest month's value off your chart, then report it in an f-string. For example:

```python
coldest = -22.9         # January's value, read from the chart
print(f"Toolik's coldest month averages about {coldest} degrees Celsius.")
```

Now write one more sentence comparing it to the warmest month.
:::

## Step 7: Export 💾

**Export** means saving your results so you or a collaborator can use them later. This is the
foundation of reproducible science. `monthly_means.to_csv(...)` writes your summary to a file.

✅ **Canonical cell. Copy and run it exactly (in your notebook):**

```python
monthly_means.to_csv("monthly_means.csv", header=True)
```

Open the file browser in JupyterLab and you will find `monthly_means.csv`. It looks like this:

```csv
Month,Daily_AirTemp_Mean_C
1,-22.89
2,-20.70
3,-20.69
4,-11.76
5,-0.80
6,8.59
```

:::{.callout-tip title="🔁 Change one thing"}
Change only the file name. Pick one and re-save:

- `monthly_means.to_csv("monthly_temps.csv", header=True)`
- `monthly_means.to_csv("toolik_monthly.csv", header=True)`
- `monthly_means.to_csv("my_results.csv", header=True)`

Same data, new file. Your `monthly_means` in memory stays the same.
:::

:::{.callout-tip title="✍️ Say it in a sentence (optional)"}
Name what you saved. For example, set `filename = "monthly_means.csv"` and then print
`f"I saved my results to {filename}."`
:::

## Naming the whole game: the 10-step workflow

You just did it. Here is the workflow you played through, named in full. Every analysis in this
course, and in your career, is some path through these ten steps:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A["1. Import 📂"] --> B["2. Explore 🔍"] --> C["3. Clean 🧹"]
    C --> D["4. Filter 🎯"] --> E["5. Sort 📊"] --> F["6. Transform 🔧"]
    F --> G["7. Group 👥"] --> H["8. Aggregate 📈"] --> I["9. Join / Reshape 🔗"]
    I --> J["10. Visualize 📊"]
```

Today you traveled Import → Explore → Group → Aggregate → Visualize → Export, skipping the steps
we have not taught yet. That is normal. Few analyses use every step, and they always happen in
this order.

📖 **Read more:** [The Data Science Workflow](../the-data-science-workflow.qmd) gives a
one-sentence description of each step and shows which day you will learn it.

## 🗓️ Coming Attractions

Every "code stranger" you met today becomes a friend on a specific day:

| Step | What it does | You'll learn it on |
|------|--------------|--------------------|
| 1. Import | Load data into a DataFrame | **Day 2** |
| 2. Explore | Get to know the table | **Day 2** |
| 3. Clean | Fix missing values, types, duplicates | **Day 4** |
| 4. Filter | Keep only the rows you want | **Day 3** |
| 5. Sort | Order rows by a column | **Day 3** |
| 6. Transform | Build new columns | **Day 4** |
| 7. Group | Split rows into buckets by a key | **Day 5** |
| 8. Aggregate | Collapse each bucket to a number | **Day 5** |
| 9. Join / Reshape | Combine tables; add a time dimension | **Day 6** |
| 10. Visualize | Turn numbers into pictures | **Day 7** |

## Key Points

- Visualize with `plt.plot()` and `plt.bar()`. Label with `plt.title()`, `plt.xlabel()`, and
  `plt.ylabel()`. Today you change labels only.
- Export results with `.to_csv("filename.csv")` so your work is saved and reproducible.
- The complete ten-step workflow is Import, Explore, Clean, Filter, Sort, Transform, Group,
  Aggregate, Join/Reshape, and Visualize.
- You now know the shape of the whole course. Each of the next six days teaches a piece of this
  same workflow.
